title: The 10 Best Corded Drills
subtitle: Wired drills ranked from live Amazon data — endless power for the least money, no battery to die.
intro: Cordless drills get all the attention, but a corded drill still wins on two things: it never runs out of charge, and it delivers full torque for the least money. Plug it in and it just keeps going — ideal for big mixing jobs, long sessions, or a drill you leave on the bench for years without worrying about a dead battery. This list covers corded drill/drivers and hammer drills (which add a pounding action for masonry). If you want to drill anywhere with no cord, see the cordless drills instead.
data_source: Amazon product listings on the data_captured date. Prices, ratings and review counts change daily; check the listing before relying on a number.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER DR260C 5.5-Amp 3/8" Corded Drill
products.best_for: A reliable, cheap drill for everyday jobs around the house.
products.verdict: The value legend, and the highest-scoring corded drill here. 7,700 reviews at 4.6 stars, a keyless chuck, and variable-speed reversible control for around $44. The one to buy if you just need a reliable drill.
pros: Most-reviewed corded drill here — 7,700 ratings at 4.6 stars
cons: 5.5 amps is light for heavy drilling

products.name: BLACK+DECKER BEHD201 6.5-Amp 1/2" Corded Hammer Drill
products.best_for: An occasional concrete anchor or brick hole for about $54.
products.verdict: The affordable way into a corded hammer drill. A 6.5-amp motor with a hammer mode for the occasional concrete anchor or brick, backed by 2,200 reviews for around $54.
cons: 6.5 amps is modest for heavy masonry
4.3 stars, a step below the leaders

products.name: DEWALT DWD210G 8-Amp 3/8" Corded Drill (mid-handle)
products.best_for: Regular drilling with big bits, where the mid-handle gives control.
products.verdict: The best corded drill for most people. A strong 8-amp motor, a comfortable mid-handle grip for control on big bits, and the highest rating here at 4.8 stars. Pure DEWALT reliability that'll outlast a decade of batteries.
pros: Mid-handle grip for control and torque
cons: Keyed chuck (a chuck key to keep track of)

products.name: BLACK+DECKER DR560 7-Amp 1/2" Drill/Driver Kit
products.best_for: Driving fasteners and turning big bits, with a torque-geared 1/2 in keyless chuck.
products.verdict: A 7-amp, 1/2-inch drill/driver with a keyless chuck and a lower top speed geared for torque — good for driving fasteners and big bits. A well-rated BLACK+DECKER at a fair price.
pros: Torque-geared for driving and big bits

products.name: Hammerhead 7.5-Amp 1/2" Corded Hammer Drill (6-pc)
products.best_for: Occasional drilling and light masonry on the smallest budget.
products.verdict: The cheapest drill on this list at $39.95: a 7.5-amp hammer drill with a 6-piece bit set and 2,300 reviews behind it. Not refined, but fine for occasional drilling and light masonry.

products.name: DEWALT DWE1014 7-Amp 3/8" Corded Drill (keyed chuck)
products.best_for: Users who want a keyed chuck's grip on bits and a 7-amp DEWALT motor.
products.verdict: A no-nonsense 7-amp DEWALT with a keyed chuck for maximum bit grip. Smooth, durable, and well-rated over 1,100 reviews — a great pick if you prefer a keyed chuck's holding power.
pros: 7-amp motor, keyed chuck grips bits hard

products.name: DEWALT DWD520K 10-Amp 1/2" Corded Hammer Drill Kit
products.best_for: Concrete, brick and big holes, where a 10-amp hammer drill earns its price.
products.verdict: The most powerful drill on the list, and the one to buy if price is no object. A 10-amp hammer drill that bores through concrete and masonry, ships in a kit with a case, and carries DEWALT's build and warranty.
pros: Big 10-amp motor with hammer mode for masonry
Comes as a kit with a carry case
cons: By far the most expensive here
Overkill for wood and light drilling

products.name: GALAX PRO 5-Amp 1/2" Corded Hammer Drill with 105 Accessories
products.best_for: Hanging shelves and setting wall anchors, with bits, anchors and a case in the box.
products.verdict: A 5-amp hammer drill sold as a kit: 105 accessories (drill bits, screwdriver bits, wall anchors with screws), a depth gauge, an auxiliary handle and a carrying case. It suits light home jobs where you want everything in one box.
pros: 105 accessories and a carrying case included
Hammer and drill modes on one switch
Speed-setting dial plus variable trigger, 0-3,000 rpm
cons: 5-amp motor, the smallest on this list

products.name: SKIL DL181901 7.5-Amp 1/2" Corded Drill
products.best_for: Spade bits and hole saws on a budget, thanks to the 1/2 in chuck.
products.verdict: A 7.5-amp, 1/2-inch corded drill that takes bigger bits than the 3/8" models — good for spade bits and hole saws. Solid SKIL value at just over $50.
pros: Handles bigger bits and hole saws

products.name: SKIL HD182001 7.5-Amp 1/2" Corded Hammer Drill
products.best_for: A mid-priced hammer drill with more motor than the BLACK+DECKER.
products.verdict: SKIL's 7.5-amp corded hammer drill — more motor than the BLACK+DECKER for a similar price, with a hammer mode for masonry. A capable mid-range pick.

avoid.name: No-name 9-Amp 1050W 1/2" Corded Impact Hammer Drill
avoid.flag: Lowest-rated, with a 9A/1050W claim its reviews don't back up
avoid.verdict: The lowest-rated corded drill here at 3.3 stars, from a no-name seller, with a '9 AMP / 1050W' spec that outruns DEWALT's flagship on paper — but not in the reviews, where buyers report weak, rough performance.
reasons: 3.3 stars is the lowest rating in the category — buyers report it bogs down, rattles, and doesn't match its numbers.
The '9 amp / 1050W' headline is bigger than any name-brand drill on this list, which is a red flag on a $35 tool: the spec is doing marketing work the motor can't.
No brand, no warranty, no support — listings like this appear and vanish under new names.
For $5 more the Hammerhead 7.5A gives you a real hammer drill with 2,300 reviews behind it.

buyers_guide.a: A corded drill never runs out of charge and gives full torque for the least money — great for long sessions, mixing paint or mortar, and a keep-forever bench drill. The trade is the cord and needing an outlet. Want to drill anywhere? See the cordless list.

A regular drill/driver bores wood, metal, and plastic and drives screws. A hammer drill adds a rapid pounding action for drilling into concrete, brick, and masonry. If you'll never touch masonry, save money and skip the hammer feature.

A 3/8" chuck fits most common bits and spins faster — best for general drilling and driving. A 1/2" chuck accepts larger bits (spade bits, hole saws, big masonry bits) and usually has more low-end torque. Bigger jobs, get 1/2".

A keyless chuck lets you swap bits by hand — fast and convenient. A keyed chuck grips slightly harder for heavy drilling but needs the chuck key (which you'll eventually lose). For most people, keyless wins.

For a corded drill, amps roughly track power. 5-6 amps is fine for light home drilling; 7-8 amps handles general work and bigger bits; 10 amps is heavy-duty hammer-drill territory. Ignore inflated wattage claims on no-name tools.
